title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
description: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.The histori
body: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.The historic meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters."The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing are yet to comment.No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior American official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025."President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation which helped to resolve the Cold War.The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement which included China, which has been building up its arsenal.Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could turn up major hurdles and take years.

schema.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says

title: What we know about the longest US nationwide flight ground stoppage since 9/11
description: Figure caption, US ground stop caused by 'incredibly old air traffic control system', Duffy saysByGrace Eliza GoodwinUpdated 34 minutes agoThe US Fede
body: Figure caption, US ground stop caused by 'incredibly old air traffic control system', Duffy saysByGrace Eliza GoodwinUpdated 34 minutes agoThe US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and that everybody was safe.Here's what we know.How many flights were affected?The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.The Federal Aviation Administration opened skies again at until 20:15 EST.Figure caption, 'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stopWhat about international flights?All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended "on request of the FAA due to technical issues", according to Eurocontrol's website.There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK, Ukraine, and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, grounded all US-bound flights until further notice.Air Canada cancelled flights between the US and Canada.When will normal service resume?Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference on Friday night that the outage would cause a ripple effect for a few days."It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.Tens of thousands of people were stranded in airports around the country, many of them "without any knowledge of where they're going to sleep tonight", Duffy said.Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations. American Airlines said it was "focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening". JetBlue said it would resume flights on Saturday morning. Image source, EPAImage caption, Luggage from cancelled flights at Ronald Reagan airportWhat caused the ground stop?Duffy said a legacy air traffic control communications system became overloaded."So this is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down," Duffy said.He said this had affected communications and radar. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said, estimating a $50 billion price tag."It's going to continue to fail," he said.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the news conference said they had seen "zero evidence" it was a cyber-attack.He also ruled out any link to the global Microsoft outage that began on Thursday.Mullin said the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system had overwhelmed it.Both cabinet secretaries insisted the public was never in danger during the stoppage.When was the last ground stop?It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001."This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.Dr Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system."That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published, and flights were grounded until that system was restored.But Friday's incident lasted longer than the 2023 event.

schema.headline: What we know about the longest US nationwide flight ground stoppage since 9/11

title: US Air Force says it responded to 'suspected drones' over RAF Lakenheath
description: The US Air Force said it responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity" over RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk on Friday evening.No personnel, aircraft
body: The US Air Force said it responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity" over RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk on Friday evening.No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a spokesperson for the US Air Force said.It comes after unconfirmed reports that sirens were sounded at the base, which residents reported hearing from a nearby village. A Ministry of Defence spokesperson told the BBC it was "coordinating with all relevant parties", adding that US Air Force security personnel responded to the reports and the situation was resolved."We are working closely with them to establish the facts," they added.West Suffolk MP Nick Timothy said he had been in touch with authorities at the base, and was told "there is no threat to the public, and the incident is now resolved"."Given the raised threat level, I continue to encourage everyone to report anything suspicious or out of the ordinary to the authorities," he added in a social media post.Earlier this week, at least 12 US Air Force aircraft departed the nearby RAF Mildenhall base.They included two Boeing Stratotanker KC-135 refuelling aircraft, with one apparently headed towards Germany and another seen landing at Prestwick Airport near Glasgow.There has been heightened security activity at US bases in the UK following an incident at RAF Fairford in September that Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran played a part in.Police said petrol but no explosives were found during searches of vans near the base. Two men have been charged by the Crown Prosecution Service over their alleged involvement in the incident. While Iran denied any responsibility, the US removed all of its bombers from the base in October.The Wall Street Journal reported the departure of the US aircraft from RAF Mildenhall this week was in response to a further threat from Iran but the BBC has not independently verified the claim.Earlier this week, Downing Street insisted British airbases were safe and that their security is a "top priority".RAF Lakenheath hosts the US Air Force's 48th Fighter Wing, or the Liberty Wing as it is also known, which has nearly 7,000 active-duty personnel, some of whom are stationed at the base. The Liberty Wing is the largest US fighter operation in Europe, its website says, employing four combat ready fighter squadrons.

schema.headline: US Air Force says it responded to 'suspected drones' over RAF Lakenheath

title: Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore
description: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economyByTess
body: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economyByTessa Wong and Osmond ChiaReporting fromSingaporeA major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.Megaspeed is a case in point.It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.The city-state has had some success in policing this.It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Megaspeed's office in Singapore In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud. In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity. On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meetingHow Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man. During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Alice Huang, seen here in Taipei with Jensen Huang last year, ran Megaspeed for several months in 2023All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore."For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said."Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China"."This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

schema.headline: Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore

title: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
description: Image source, Rockstar Games / Take-Two InteractiveImage caption, GTA 6 will feature brand new protagonists Jason and Lucia - the first playable femal
body: Image source, Rockstar Games / Take-Two InteractiveImage caption, GTA 6 will feature brand new protagonists Jason and Lucia - the first playable female character in any of the 3D gamesByLaura CressTechnology reporterAfter a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks, the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment."We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.Image caption, Brian Baglow (left) and Dave Jones, worked on the original Grand Theft AutoThe original Grand Theft Auto was released in 1997 in Dundee, Scotland by DMA Design, a relatively small team, at least judging by later games' standards.Following its success with puzzle game Lemmings, the studio was toying around with the idea of making a racing game, initially called Race'n'Chase.Sitting in the state-of-the-art computer lab at Dundee's Abertay University decades on, Jones tells me the developers still felt they had to bring something new to the table."At DMA, we always wanted to do something different," he says. "What was the unique spin we could put on it?"Part of the answer, he said, came in what feels like a premise gamers take for granted now - "just getting out of the car".He says the idea of being able to not only drive but switch and steal cars, running about on foot as you did so, meant "all of a sudden you had this interesting mix of gaming coming together".Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, DMA Design / BMG InteractiveImage caption, The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997 and featured a top-down view in 2DSlide 1 of 7, A screenshot from the original Grand Theft Auto. The words BUSTED! is shown in yellow. A top down view shows several police cars with sirens on and a red car with door open, and a person on the road., The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997 and featured a top-down view in 2D'More fun' playing the bad guyThe team envisioned a game, Jones says, where you could play as both a criminal and a police officer. But he quickly reconsidered the second option, as it would require players to behave "by the book"."At some point we just said, you know what, it's way more fun playing the bad guy, so that's what the game was about," he adds.Despite some of these novel approaches to the game's design, Jones says it was a "slow burn" in sales compared with Lemmings - partly because you had to "play it to get it"."For the whole of the year that GTA came out, it just kept going and selling and selling," says Baglow."And we reckoned it was the word of mouth. The people who had played it going, oh my God, have you played this game?"Its themes of criminality and violence sparked controversy - leading to debates in the UK Parliament and calls to ban the game. Yet it later transpired much of that  was generated by the game's own publisher, BMG Interactive, as a viral marketing stunt."We just did things that we felt were fun," says Jones. "We never at any point kind of thought, should we do that? Is it controversial? We never thought that way."Although relatively basic in appearance, with its top-down 2D view and more arcade-like graphics, the original game forged the blueprint for the series' signature satire still seen in much later, more advanced GTAs today.Despite being set in an exaggerated version of American cities, its Scottishness could still be found in its humour and its outsider perspective, says Guardian video games editor Keza MacDonald."It's a deeply satirical game," she says. "It really takes aim at the hyper-individualist, hyper-capitalist nature of the US."Partly out of necessity due to their comparatively low budget and the cost of real-world licenses, the team came up with cheeky brand names and fake radio stations players could listen to while driving around and causing mayhem.Though some of these choices were made out of limitations, Baglow says the world-building is the element he's most proud of from the original, which is still a big part of what makes a title feel like GTA."It's the business names, it's the radio stations, it's the lyrics, it's the DJs," he says."Every part of that is making you believe that this environment you're in is a big cohesive whole."Image source, Rockstar Games / Take-Two InteractiveImage caption, The new game's location - the fictional state of Leonida - is expected to be double the size of GTA V's mapWhen GTA V launched in 2013, it made $1bn (£760m) in just three days - faster than any entertainment product had achieved at the time.The series evolved into a cultural reference point itself - something people recognised, understood and even referenced outside gaming."I've seen movies where someone says 'don't go all GTA on me'... it was just surreal," says Jones.MacDonald, joining me in Glasgow's gaming cafe, RCade, tells me there's an argument now that while earlier GTAs "took a lot" from the big screen, films are now "probably more influenced by GTA" than the other way round.She says later titles in the series have a cinematic feel, but also reflect the distinct identity it has forged for itself.As for why Jones believes the game has become such a cultural phenomenon, he says it's the simple fact that it's "based on real life"."It's not like a lot of games like sci-fi or adventure or fantasy," he says. "There's nothing you have to learn about it, as long as you know a city and driving."Image caption, "It means so much to so many people," says Baglow, leftGTA 6 is expected to surpass its predecessor on every level, not only in scale and scope, but also in revenue.Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history.This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it.The hype has spilt into the real world, with London's Selfridges transformed into a Vice City-themed pop-up attraction and fictional GTA brands appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game."Everyone is extremely excited for this," says MacDonald. "It's hoping to be a shot in the arm for the general games industry, but also every player is looking to see what Rockstar's been doing for all this time."It's very rare that we have this one massive game that everybody's going to be, if not playing, then certainly interested in."Do Jones and Baglow ever wish they were still working on the game now, given the huge amount of global attention focused on it?"I think everybody loves having their time on it, for one, two, three versions," Jones says."But eventually you want to go off and do other things as well."Baglow adds that watching "the rest of the world fall in love with the game over the last 29 years has just been joyful"."It means so much to so many people - it's been fantastic."

schema.headline: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6

title: Former Hamas bodyguard guilty of Birmingham knife attack
description: Image source, West Midlands PoliceImage caption, Mohammed Alfatih was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020ByPhil MackieRep
body: Image source, West Midlands PoliceImage caption, Mohammed Alfatih was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020ByPhil MackieReporting fromat Birmingham Crown CourtDaniel SandfordHome Affairs correspondent and Rushdi Abu AloufGaza correspondentA former Hamas bodyguard, wanted in Germany over an alleged plot to murder Jewish people, has been found guilty of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his UK home.Mohammed Alfatih, previously known as Mohammed Naim, was regularly seen acting as a bodyguard for a former leader of Hamas in 2006. He was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2021.The 40-year-old was found guilty by majority verdict of unlawfully wounding a bailiff who had come to repossess his wife's car, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of wounding with intent.Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terror unit at the moment he attacked the bailiff in Birmingham last year. The son of a senior Hamas official, he could not be named during his trial due to reporting restrictions.During the trial, footage was shown of Alfatih brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in the suburb of Kings Heath and trying to stab the bailiff as he drove away.He told the court he chased the victim across the street to scare him away after his wife was asked to settle her debts of more than £2,250 linked to unpaid parking fines. Her car had been clamped by the enforcement officer, who was involved in a struggle inside Alfatih's terraced home.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Alfatih, circled, was bodyguard for Ismail Haniyeh before being removed from his postJurors were not told of Alfatih's links to proscribed terrorist group Hamas or his work as a bodyguard to its now-deceased former leader Ismail Haniyeh.But it can now be revealed that while detained for the attack in Birmingham, he was re-arrested when authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged gun plot to attack Jewish targets there.It is alleged Alfatih was an organiser and was involved in the movement of weapons. German authorities also allege he had pre-recorded a video wearing a balaclava and sunglasses claiming the attack was planned on behalf of the Izzedine al-Qassam Brigades, the military wing of Hamas. The alleged attack was prevented after a tip-off from the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad.Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK.Image source, West Midlands PoliceImage caption, Alfatih faces sentencing in Birmingham on 11 JanuaryDuring his evidence, Alfatih did not mention Hamas but told the court he had been tortured for 25 days while detained in Egypt in 2010.The father-of-four, an IT worker, failed in a legal application to try to get the wounding charges thrown out on the grounds of prejudicial media coverage about the investigation in Germany. During the two-week trial at Birmingham Crown Court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October last year.Bailiff Kevin Bucknall was left with cuts to his head and required hospital treatment, but the defendant had pleaded not guilty on the grounds of self-defence.Alfatih told jurors it had happened a day after he had learned one of his brothers had been killed in Gaza. He also said while giving evidence that traumatic experiences in his past included being shot and injured on two different occasions.Image source, Der SpiegelImage caption, German prosecutors have named Alfatih in relation to extradition proceedings"I just want to be as honest as I can," he told the jury. "I don't think I was even in my full mind. I didn't intend anything other than him moving away."I wasn't anything more than terrified."Defence barrister Kate O'Raghallaigh said Alfatih had a heightened perception of danger, triggered by fear and desperation he had previously experienced.Jurors deliberated for more than six hours over three days before convicting him, with Alfatih heard mumbling to himself as the verdicts were returned. He has been in custody since the knife attack and now faces sentencing in Birmingham on 11 January, as well as separate extradition proceedings at Westminster Magistrates' Court.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Jurors were not told of Alfatih's links to proscribed terrorist group HamasThe BBC understands that when Alfatih went by the name of Naim, he enrolled in a VIP protection course and was selected to accompany Haniyeh on trips to Egypt and other countries between 2006 and 2008. However, he was later removed from the role due to his behaviour.The second son of former Hamas health minister Bassem Naim, he later spent time in Malaysia, Qatar and Turkey before arriving in Britain. Following his conviction, a government source said it was "staggering" that he was granted asylum and later given citizenship. A Home Office spokesperson added Hamas was a proscribed terrorist organisation and the government condemned "those who choose to support its activities and further its aims".Additional reporting by Josh SandifordGet in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Birmingham and the Black Country

schema.headline: Former Hamas bodyguard guilty of Birmingham knife attack

title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
description: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of
body: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow."In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week."Our proposals were almost laughed at."Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire"."The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken."Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.And what of Putin?At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.You can see why.The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine

title: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision
description: Figure caption, Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New OrleansByAna FaguySome 130 people on a cruise ship docked in Ne
body: Figure caption, Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New OrleansByAna FaguySome 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel, Atlantic Asphalt.The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort went to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help"."We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.Calls about the collision came in around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans Chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.Image source, Getty ImagesThere were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port of New Orleans.Passengers began disembarking from the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping on to its side, Mayor Moreno said.Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help and officials shut down the Mississippi River for the search effort.The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue was an "incredible job".Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the US Coast Guard also supported local rescue operations.Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.Image source, Getty ImagesShips have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what happened.Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he saw the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision."It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic."Holford added that he saw passengers and crew members "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking.The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website.Built in 2015, the vessel has at least four decks.

schema.headline: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision

title: Christmas trees: How early is too early to buy one and will it last until Christmas?
description: The appropriate time to put up your Christmas tree is a question almost as divisive as whether Yorkshire pudding has a place on the Christmas dinner p
body: The appropriate time to put up your Christmas tree is a question almost as divisive as whether Yorkshire pudding has a place on the Christmas dinner plate. Some might feel the best time is just after Bonfire Night, others may think Christmas Eve is more apt, and most will probably plump for somewhere in between. Tesco started selling Christmas trees at half-price this week and said more than 90% of its trees had sold out by the end of November last year.Lidl and some other retailers are also launching their ranges next week, while others including Dobbies Garden Centres are waiting until the last week of November.But with Christmas Day still six weeks away, is it unwise to rush into buying a real tree so early? And do you risk spending your Christmas week cleaning up piles of pine needles?Probably, says Mick Walker, from Bolton Christmas Trees, which grows trees in the Scottish Highlands before sending them to homes across the UK."It might last until the beginning of Christmas, but it won't last the full holiday," he warns. "Unless its a potted one, it's going to be sagging by Christmas Day - big time."He calls Tesco's half-price deal "insane", adding that it's "sucking them into buying something now that isn't going to do the job". So when would he suggest is the best time? "If it was me, I'd put it up a week before Christmas eve, [and it will] last straight through until New Year."The most popular Christmas trees available in the UK are the Nordmann fir variety, which are non-drop, meaning they don't drop their needles. Norway Spruce is another common variety and have a strong pine scent, but generally should be kept outdoors or put up just before Christmas.Pine trees, Walker says, have the longest lifespan, but he concedes they lack that classic Christmas look.Or, of course, you could opt for a tried-and-tested artificial tree, which is what Katie McDonald from Belfast put up in her house last week."When I was a kid my mum always waited to the last minute to let us kids put the tree up. We would be the last house on our street and the last of all our friends to get the tree up," she tells the BBC."So I made myself a wee childlike promise that when I had my own house I'd be one of the first to put my tree up."She says she will replace her artificial tree with a real one in a few weeks, so it is in prime condition come Christmas Day.

schema.headline: Christmas trees: How early is too early to buy one and will it last until Christmas?

title: Bessent blames Lutnick's department for Nvidia chip sales to Megaspeed
description: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips,
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet.Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months"."But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China."President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia."The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external."The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, accoprding to US media. Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December."Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection.A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security."Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

schema.headline: Bessent blames Lutnick's department for Nvidia chip sales to Megaspeed

title: First catch aborted in SpaceX Starship rocket double-catch test
description: The 124m-tall rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:45 local time (22:45 GMT) on Friday.It was suppos
body: The 124m-tall rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:45 local time (22:45 GMT) on Friday.It was supposed to catch the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned to the launch tower, but instead it was diverted to the ocean.During a stream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority, and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each maneuver safely."The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, is continuing its journey to space, where it is deploying 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet from space.The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off, where a second catch may be attempted.SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead, it has splashed down in the ocean.Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it is in space.If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.But it is not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

schema.headline: First catch aborted in SpaceX Starship rocket double-catch test

title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage as it reports broad recovery
description: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the wo
body: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again."We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said."We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered.A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services."The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem."Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said."In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

schema.headline: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage as it reports broad recovery

title: Probation officers to take industrial action over pay and early release scheme
description: Probation officers have voted to reject a 5% pay rise and take industrial action, citing growing pressure created by the government's prisoner early r
body: Probation officers have voted to reject a 5% pay rise and take industrial action, citing growing pressure created by the government's prisoner early release scheme.Members of Napo, the probation service union, voted to refuse overtime from 23 November - and could take strike action should the union "deem that option to be necessary".Its general secretary Ian Lawrence said the service was "already in crisis" before the early release scheme came into force, which relies on probation staff monitoring freed prisoners in the community.A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said the government had put forward a "strong offer" and was recruiting an extra "1,300 officers to significantly cut workloads".They added that the government has "robust contingency plans in place" to ensure offenders "are still subject to the same rigorous supervision" in the event of industrial action.Probation service unions have warned that officers have too many cases and the rate at which staff are leaving the profession has increased.The service has come under renewed pressure in recent months as a result of the early release scheme, the union said, which the government introduced as prisons were dangerously close to capacity. Seven-hundred eligible offenders originally sentenced to up to 19 months were released on 1 October, with another two groups of 650 prisoners released on 13 October and 10 November.Another nine groups are expected to leave prison in the next seven months, with inmates who received longer sentences included in the later cohorts. Some 250 prisoners serving more than 12 years are expected to be released on 9 June.Napo's leader said staff had tried "desperately" to implement early release schemes introduced by the Labour government and previous Conservative government, but had been asked to do so with "inadequate staff and a lack of resources". The government has said electronic tags and probation intervention will help to manage prisoners freed early. The Probation Service uses electronic monitoring to track curfews and conditions of a court or prison order, with most of those eligible for early release now requiring tagging.But a September report by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Probation (HMIP) found that almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders' movements were not fitted on time.

schema.headline: Probation officers to take industrial action over pay and early release scheme

title: Keaton Slater's parents' fight to bring Latvian killer to UK
description: Days after her 12-year-old son was killed by a BMW driver travelling at 70mph, Louise Slater sat outside the suspect's home, gathering the courage to
body: Days after her 12-year-old son was killed by a BMW driver travelling at 70mph, Louise Slater sat outside the suspect's home, gathering the courage to plead with his family to hand him in.She had been given the name and address of Aleksanders Dolars after her son Keaton was killed in a hit-and-run in Coventry.Distraught, she was preparing to knock on the door when a neighbour approached and asked what she was doing.When she explained, he told her the family, from Latvia, had packed up and left a day or two earlier.Keaton's suspected killer had fled just hours after leaving him dying in the road.What followed was a relentless two-year fight by his parents to track him down and bring him back to England to face justice.He was finally jailed on Friday, for nine years and four months.This article contains details some readers may find upsettingDolars' name had been already circulating locally before police identified him as their main suspect on 18 June 2024, four days after Keaton was killed.A family waiting at nearby traffic lights said their seven-seater "shook violently" as a BMW driver sped past at what appeared to be far more than the 30mph limit. Moments later, they saw something fly into the air behind them.The car did not stop.As it disappeared from view, the family noticed a black rucksack and a single shoe lying in Radford Road and realised a child may have been hit.Taiwo Owatemi, MP for Coventry North West, was working behind the scenes to build political support.Colleagues in Westminster had warned her that, without an extradition agreement between the UK and EU, securing Dolars' return would be extremely difficult.However, she was encouraged by the Latvian ambassador telling her his country did not want a difficult relationship with the UK, given the proximity of the country to Ukraine and its continuing war with Russia.She also learned from him that Latvians were angry at what had happened and that  Dolars was bringing shame on their country."When you have Latvians in Latvia asking for justice, when you have Latvians in the UK asking for justice, that's his number one job as ambassador," Owatemi said.Latvians were also proactive identifying where Dolars was in the country, she said.Louise said she had received messages from families there via a Facebook page set up within the community after Keaton's death.She said people were saying, "we don't want him here, he's scum".They also sent a video of Dolars happily walking around and also with his car. She sent them to police."He was free. He thought he'd got away with it," she said.In February 2026, there was a breakthrough. The Latvian government considered legislation to allow citizens to be extradited to the UK for prosecution.Campaigning by the family had helped bring about a new law where instances of extradition would now be considered on a case-by-case basis.

schema.headline: Keaton Slater's parents' fight to bring Latvian killer to UK

title: Jesus Owono: Goalkeeper gets 12-game suspension for tackle which resulted in death of Jesus de Miguel
description: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has been given a 12-match suspension by the Spanish football federation's disciplinary committee after his challenge
body: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has been given a 12-match suspension by the Spanish football federation's disciplinary committee after his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel during the closing stages of the second-tier match between their two respective sides on 2 November.De Miguel died the following day, aged 30.The disciplinary committee said it had to base its decision "on the facts expressly recorded in the referee's report", which stated the player "was sent off for 'violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play'."The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, is public knowledge."The committee added the "nature of the conduct described and the accompanying circumstances" means that "the maximum sanction, a 12-match suspension, is justified".Separately, the federation has decided the game between the two sides, which was abandoned seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred, will not be replayed."This avoids having to resume play from the precise moment at which the tragic incident occurred," it said.The teams were drawing 2-2 at the time and that result will now stand, with a federation committee saying that was the "most respectful course of action, given the extraordinary and tragic circumstances of this case".Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on 4 November, in which he said he was experiencing "the most difficult days" of his life and felt "enormous pain" about De Miguel's death.On Thursday, FC Andorra manager Carles Manso said Equatorial Guinea international Owono is yet to decide whether he will return to football following the incident.Manso said Owono is currently spending time with his family and is "completely free to make any decision" with regard to a potential return, adding: "What we have to do is support him in every way and be close to ​him."We will ​give him space so that he feels completely free to make ‌any ⁠decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return."When he feels it is appropriate and when ​he feels genuinely ready to take a ​decision ⁠like that [he will do so]."

schema.headline: Jesus Owono: Goalkeeper gets 12-game suspension for tackle which resulted in death of Jesus de Miguel
